activities.caption: true or false — the household counts
activities.name: demogCountsJudge

statements.s: One-person households are roughly a third of households in much of Europe.
statements.why: The growth story of the rich world — and nearly two-fifths in Japan, where they became the largest single category in the 2010s.

statements.s: Solo living multiplies housing demand, appliances and energy per head.
statements.why: A statistic family sociology missed until demography priced it.

statements.s: Roughly a quarter of children in the US and UK live with one parent — against under a tenth in much of continental Europe.
statements.why: Policy and norms, not biology, explain the gap.

statements.s: The extended family type has disappeared worldwide.
statements.why: The proportions shifted, not the forms — multigenerational living persists or grows across much of Asia, Africa and southern Europe, and has been rising in the US for decades.

activities.caption: the 4-2-1 care debt — follow the demand
activities.name: demog421Branch

config.root: The '4-2-1' structure: one child potentially responsible for two parents and four grandparents — a demographic debt booked by the one-child policy (1979–2015). The care demand now arrives. Follow where it goes:

start.text: Where does the care migrate to?

choices.label: To the state
choices.feedback: Partly — pensions and schools took some of the family's functions. But the migration is incomplete everywhere.

choices.label: To the market
choices.feedback: Partly — childcare moved there. Paid care has limits of its own, and the demand keeps outgrowing it.

choices.label: Back onto the family
choices.feedback: This is where most of it lands: the largest unpaid care provider on earth — whose capacity is shrinking precisely as demand rises.

state.text: The state can legislate pensions and schools; the informal care they cannot legislate into existence stays somewhere else.

market.text: The market prices care; what it does not price falls back on households — the old-age dependency ratio roughly halves in most rich countries by 2050.

family.text: The informal care the arithmetic implies cannot simply be legislated or purchased into existence — the functions migrated, incompletely, and the remainder is the debt coming due.

config.why: The family's functions did not disappear with modernisation; they migrated — partly to the state, partly to the market — and the migration is incomplete everywhere.

activities.anchor: The critics sharpened the model rather than demolishing it
activities.caption: pair each theorist with the claim
activities.name: demogTheoristsMatch

config.prompt: The family-functions debate — pair each voice:

pairs.right: four universal functions: sexual, reproductive, economic, educational
the industrial nuclear family: a geographically mobile workforce needs small, portable units
the functions rest on unpaid, unequally distributed domestic labour
conjugal roles converging as wives entered paid work
functions listed from outside miss what families mean to their members

config.why: The debate is the topic's live form: is the family defined by what it does for society, or by what its members do for each other — and can demography even see the second question?

activities.anchor: it is worth walking its stages
activities.caption: place the stage-one rates
activities.name: demogStagePlace

config.prompt: Stage one of the transition, pre-transition: birth and death rates both sit around what level, per 1,000 per year?
config.why: Around 35–40 per 1,000 per year each — so populations barely grow. Then mortality falls in years while fertility falls in decades: the timing mismatch that created the twentieth century's population explosion.

config.text: South Korea's total fertility rate hit %%0%% in %%1%% — barely a third of replacement (%%2%%) — while over half the world's countries now sit below replacement, and the UN's 2024 projection peaks near %%3%% billion in the mid-2080s.
config.hint: The lowest fertility ever recorded, its year, the replacement level, and the projected peak.

activities.anchor: The rise was real; the attribution is contested
activities.caption: call the policy's price tag
activities.name: demogHungaryEst

config.prompt: Hungary runs the world's most expensive attempt to bend the fertility curve. Roughly what share of GDP does it spend on family support?
config.why: Around 5% — income-tax exemption for mothers of four, subsidised loans cancelled per child. The fertility path rose from 1.23 (2011) to about 1.6 (2021), then slipped back toward 1.3 by 2025; the sober lesson: policy can remove obstacles, but no intervention has yet recreated the family systems that once produced replacement fertility on their own.
config.context: Timing shifts can lift the period rate for years without changing completed family size.

activities.anchor: the mechanism was mostly not medicine
activities.caption: drag between 1850 and today
activities.name: demogLifeExpCompare

config.prompt: Global life expectancy, then and now — drag the divider:

before.label: Mid-nineteenth century
before.text: Near 30 years worldwide — pandemics and famine dominant, infant and child mortality doing most of the dragging.

after.label: Today
after.text: Above 73 (WHO) — chronic degenerative disease the dominant killer, and societies reaching old age before prosperity (Nigeria's median age is about 18: growing old before growing rich).

config.why: The big gains came from clean water, sanitation, nutrition and (later) vaccination collapsing infant and child mortality — a death at age 1 costs more expectancy than a death at 70. Omran's epidemiological transition names the sequence.

future migration — the widest uncertainty band
